claim: Large spines are stable and important for memory trace formation.
source: Large spines are stable and important for memory trace formation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about large spines.

claim: The majority of large spines contain synaptopodin (SP).
source: The majority of large spines also contains synaptopodin (SP), an actin-modulating and plasticity-related protein.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Synaptopodin is an actin-modulating and plasticity-related protein.
source: The majority of large spines also contains synaptopodin (SP), an actin-modulating and plasticity-related protein.
evidence: This characterization of SP is stated in the abstract.

claim: SP stabilizes F-actin.
source: Since SP stabilizes F-actin, we speculated that the presence of SP within large spines could explain their long lifetime.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of SP in the abstract.

claim: Spines containing SP survived considerably longer than spines of equal size without SP.
source: Indeed, using 2-photon time-lapse imaging of SP-transgenic granule cells in mouse organotypic tissue cultures we found that spines containing SP survived considerably longer than spines of equal size without SP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 2-photon imaging experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: SP-positive spines that underwent pruning first lost SP before disappearing.
source: Of note, SP-positive (SP+) spines that underwent pruning first lost SP before disappearing.
evidence: This is a key observation from the time-lapse imaging data reported in the abstract.

claim: The survival time courses of SP+ spines followed conditional two-stage decay functions.
source: Whereas the survival time courses of SP+ spines followed conditional two-stage decay functions, SP-negative (SP-) spines and all spines of SP-deficient animals showed single-phase exponential decays.
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling of the survival data reported in the abstract.

claim: SP-negative spines showed single-phase exponential decays.
source: Whereas the survival time courses of SP+ spines followed conditional two-stage decay functions, SP-negative (SP-) spines and all spines of SP-deficient animals showed single-phase exponential decays.
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling of the survival data reported in the abstract.

claim: All spines of SP-deficient animals showed single-phase exponential decays.
source: Whereas the survival time courses of SP+ spines followed conditional two-stage decay functions, SP-negative (SP-) spines and all spines of SP-deficient animals showed single-phase exponential decays.
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with SP-deficient mice reported in the abstract.

claim: SP clusters stabilize spines.
source: These results implicate SP as a major regulator of long-term spine stability: SP clusters stabilize spines, and the presence of SP indicates spines of high stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results stated in the abstract.

claim: The presence of SP indicates spines of high stability.
source: These results implicate SP as a major regulator of long-term spine stability: SP clusters stabilize spines, and the presence of SP indicates spines of high stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results stated in the abstract.

claim: Dendritic spines are protrusions found on the majority of excitatory neurons in vertebrate brains.
source: Dendritic spines are protrusions found on the majority of excitatory neurons in vertebrate brains.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Dendritic spines form characteristic axo-spinous synapses.
source: They form characteristic axo-spinous synapses and play an important role in integrating afferent synaptic activity with postsynaptic activity (Yuste and Denk, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation in the introduction.

claim: Dendritic spines play an important role in integrating afferent synaptic activity with postsynaptic activity.
source: They form characteristic axo-spinous synapses and play an important role in integrating afferent synaptic activity with postsynaptic activity (Yuste and Denk, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation in the introduction.

claim: The length of the spine neck has been linked to the biochemical and electrical isolation of the spine compartment.
source: While the length of the spine neck has been linked to the biochemical and electrical isolation of the spine compartment (Yuste et al., 2000; Yuste, 2013), the size of the spine head has been positively correlated with AMPA-receptor density, synaptic strength and spine stability (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: The size of the spine head has been positively correlated with AMPA-receptor density, synaptic strength and spine stability.
source: While the length of the spine neck has been linked to the biochemical and electrical isolation of the spine compartment (Yuste et al., 2000; Yuste, 2013), the size of the spine head has been positively correlated with AMPA-receptor density, synaptic strength and spine stability (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: A critical role of spines in learning, memory formation and cognition has been discussed.
source: At the behavioral level, a critical role of spines in learning, memory formation and cognition has been discussed (Segal, 2005; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010; Roberts et al., 2010) and, indeed, a recent study has shown that spines are both necessary and sufficient for memory storage and memory trace formation (Abdou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: Spines are both necessary and sufficient for memory storage and memory trace formation.
source: At the behavioral level, a critical role of spines in learning, memory formation and cognition has been discussed (Segal, 2005; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010; Roberts et al., 2010) and, indeed, a recent study has shown that spines are both necessary and sufficient for memory storage and memory trace formation (Abdou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study in the introduction.

claim: The spine apparatus consists of stacked endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: A cellular organelle unique to spines is the spine apparatus (Gray, 1959; Spacek, 1985), which consists of stacked endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and which modifies spine Ca2+ transients (Korkotian and Segal, 2011) and second messenger dynamics (Cugno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: The spine apparatus modifies spine Ca2+ transients.
source: A cellular organelle unique to spines is the spine apparatus (Gray, 1959; Spacek, 1985), which consists of stacked endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and which modifies spine Ca2+ transients (Korkotian and Segal, 2011) and second messenger dynamics (Cugno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: The spine apparatus modifies second messenger dynamics.
source: A cellular organelle unique to spines is the spine apparatus (Gray, 1959; Spacek, 1985), which consists of stacked endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and which modifies spine Ca2+ transients (Korkotian and Segal, 2011) and second messenger dynamics (Cugno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: Synaptopodin is an essential component of the spine apparatus and is required for its formation.
source: Synaptopodin (SP; GenBank accession number: NM_001109975.1) is an essential component of the spine apparatus and is required for its formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: SP is found in a 100 kDa isoform in telencephalic neurons.
source: It is an actin-modulating protein found in a 100 kDa isoform in telencephalic neurons and a 110 kDa isoform in kidney podocytes (Mundel et al., 1997; Asanuma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP is found in a 110 kDa isoform in kidney podocytes.
source: It is an actin-modulating protein found in a 100 kDa isoform in telencephalic neurons and a 110 kDa isoform in kidney podocytes (Mundel et al., 1997; Asanuma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP is almost linear because of its high proline content.
source: SP is almost linear because of its high proline content and contains several phosphorylation sites and two PPXY motifs for protein-protein interactions (Mundel et al., 1997; Asanuma et al., 2005; Asanuma et al., 2006; Faul et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP contains several phosphorylation sites and two PPXY motifs for protein-protein interactions.
source: SP is almost linear because of its high proline content and contains several phosphorylation sites and two PPXY motifs for protein-protein interactions (Mundel et al., 1997; Asanuma et al., 2005; Asanuma et al., 2006; Faul et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: Expression of SP in mice starts postnatally.
source: Expression of SP in mice starts postnatally (Mundel et al., 1997; Czarnecki et al., 2005), increases with maturation (Czarnecki et al., 2005) and declines with age (Sidhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP expression increases with maturation.
source: Expression of SP in mice starts postnatally (Mundel et al., 1997; Czarnecki et al., 2005), increases with maturation (Czarnecki et al., 2005) and declines with age (Sidhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP expression declines with age.
source: Expression of SP in mice starts postnatally (Mundel et al., 1997; Czarnecki et al., 2005), increases with maturation (Czarnecki et al., 2005) and declines with age (Sidhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP-deficient mice show deficits in synaptic plasticity.
source: SP-deficient mice show deficits in synaptic plasticity (Deller et al., 2003; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2013b; Zhang et al., 2013; Korkotian et al., 2014; Jedlicka and Deller, 2017) and adult SP-deficient mice show impaired spatial learning (Deller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: Adult SP-deficient mice show impaired spatial learning.
source: SP-deficient mice show deficits in synaptic plasticity (Deller et al., 2003; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2013b; Zhang et al., 2013; Korkotian et al., 2014; Jedlicka and Deller, 2017) and adult SP-deficient mice show impaired spatial learning (Deller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP affects the actin spinoskeleton either directly by stabilizing F-actin or indirectly via binding to alpha-actinin-2, Cdc42, RhoA, or myosin V.
source: SP also affects the actin spinoskeleton either directly by stabilizing F-actin (Mundel et al., 1997; Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008) or indirectly via binding to alpha-actinin-2, Cdc42, RhoA, or myosin V (Asanuma et al., 2005; Kremerskothen et al., 2005; Asanuma et al., 2006; Faul et al., 2007; Yanagida-Asanuma et al., 2007; Jedlicka and Deller, 2017; Konietzny et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP, via its connection to the actin cytoskeleton, is likely also connected to the post-synaptic density (PSD).
source: It is likely that SP, via its connection to the actin cytoskeleton, is also connected to the post-synaptic density (PSD), which plays an important role in synaptic stabilization (El-Husseini et al., 2000; Ehrlich et al., 2007; Yoshihara et al., 2009; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations in the introduction.

claim: The PSD plays an important role in synaptic stabilization.
source: It is likely that SP, via its connection to the actin cytoskeleton, is also connected to the post-synaptic density (PSD), which plays an important role in synaptic stabilization (El-Husseini et al., 2000; Ehrlich et al., 2007; Yoshihara et al., 2009; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: SP has been suggested to influence the geometry and stability of spines.
source: Accordingly, SP has been suggested to influence the geometry and stability of spines (Deller et al., 2000a).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion from a cited study in the introduction.

claim: Short-term imaging experiments implicated SP in plasticity-induced spine head expansion.
source: Indeed, short-term imaging experiments performed in dissociated cultures (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Vlachos et al., 2009; Konietzny et al., 2019) and acute slices (Zhang et al., 2013) implicated SP in plasticity-induced spine head expansion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the introduction.

claim: There were no differences in average spine head sizes between wildtype and SP-deficient granule cells in vivo.
source: Accordingly, we analyzed and compared spine head size in Alexa568-filled wildtype and mutant granule cells (Figure 1A,B) but could neither detect differences in average spine head sizes (Figure 1C) nor in spine head size distributions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of fixed tissue shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There were no differences in spine head size distributions between wildtype and SP-deficient granule cells in vivo.
source: Accordingly, we analyzed and compared spine head size in Alexa568-filled wildtype and mutant granule cells (Figure 1A,B) but could neither detect differences in average spine head sizes (Figure 1C) nor in spine head size distributions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of fixed tissue shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SP clusters are found in approximately 14% of spines in vivo.
source: Using Alexa 568-injected granule cells from eGFP-SP-tg mouse brain (Figure 1E; Vlachos et al., 2013a), we first studied the fraction of SP-positive spines and found SP clusters in ~14% of spines (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of fixed tissue shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Spines containing SP (SP+) were significantly larger than spines without SP (SP-) in vivo.
source: Spines containing SP (SP+) were significantly larger than spines without SP (SP-) (Figure 1G) and showed a right-shifted cumulative frequency distribution (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of fixed tissue shown in Figure 1G.

claim: SP+ spines showed a right-shifted cumulative frequency distribution compared to SP- spines in vivo.
source: Spines containing SP (SP+) were significantly larger than spines without SP (SP-) (Figure 1G) and showed a right-shifted cumulative frequency distribution (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of fixed tissue shown in Figure 1H.

claim: SP cluster size was positively correlated with spine head size in vivo.
source: In addition, SP cluster size was positively correlated with spine head size (Figure 1I), demonstrating that large SP clusters are typically found in large spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Large SP clusters are typically found in large spines in vivo.
source: In addition, SP cluster size was positively correlated with spine head size (Figure 1I), demonstrating that large SP clusters are typically found in large spines.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: SP is either not a major regulator of spine head size or its loss is compensated for in the SP-deficient mouse.
source: We conclude from these observations, that SP is indeed tightly correlated with spine size. However, lack of SP did not affect average spine head size, suggesting that SP is either not a major regulator of spine head size or that its loss is compensated for in the SP-deficient mouse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that SP-deficient mice have normal spine head sizes despite SP being associated with large spines.

claim: SP clusters were abundant in the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus in organotypic tissue cultures.
source: In these cultures SP clusters were abundant in the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus (Figure 2A), similar to what has been described for wildtype animals after SP immunolabeling (Deller et al., 2000b; Bas Orth et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an observation from the tissue culture experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SP+ spines in organotypic tissue cultures contained SP-positive spine apparatus organelles.
source: SP+ spines also contained SP-positive spine apparatus organelles (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SP-mRNA expression levels in granule cells of eGFP-SP-tg cultures were similar to SP-mRNA expression levels in granule cells of SP wildtype cultures.
source: SP-mRNA expression levels in granule cells of eGFP-SP-tg cultures were similar to SP-mRNA expression levels in granule cells of SP wildtype cultures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Average spine head size was not significantly different between eGFP-SP-tg and SP-deficient cultures.
source: In line with the results obtained in vivo (Figure 1C,D), average spine head size and spine head size distribution were not significantly different between these and SP-deficient cultures (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of tissue cultures shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Spine head size distribution was not significantly different between eGFP-SP-tg and SP-deficient cultures.
source: In line with the results obtained in vivo (Figure 1C,D), average spine head size and spine head size distribution were not significantly different between these and SP-deficient cultures (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of tissue cultures shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Approximately 8% of all granule cell spines are SP+ in organotypic tissue cultures.
source: Next, we analyzed the fraction of SP+ and SP− spines and found that approximately 8% of all granule cell spines are SP+ (Figure 2G) and ~6.4% of all granule cell spines contained a spine apparatus organelle (not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of tissue cultures shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Approximately 6.4% of all granule cell spines contained a spine apparatus organelle in organotypic tissue cultures.
source: Next, we analyzed the fraction of SP+ and SP− spines and found that approximately 8% of all granule cell spines are SP+ (Figure 2G) and ~6.4% of all granule cell spines contained a spine apparatus organelle (not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of tissue cultures.

claim: SP+ spines are on average much larger than SP- spines in organotypic tissue cultures (SP- spines: 0.364 ± 0.005 µm2; SP+ spines: 0.801 ± 0.029 µm2).
source: Analysis of head sizes of SP+ and SP− spines (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) revealed that SP+ spines are on average much larger than SP- spines (SP- spines: 0.364 ± 0.005 µm2; SP+ spines: 0.801 ± 0.029 µm2; Figure 2H), similar to what we had observed in vivo (c.f. Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of tissue cultures shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The population of SP+ spines is right-shifted toward larger spine head sizes compared to SP- spines in organotypic tissue cultures.
source: Likewise, cumulative frequency diagrams showed that the population of SP+ spines is right-shifted toward larger spine head sizes compared to SP- spines (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of tissue cultures shown in Figure 2I.

claim: There is a positive correlation between SP cluster size and spine head size in organotypic tissue cultures.
source: Finally, correlation analysis of SP cluster size and spine head size demonstrated a positive correlation between the two parameters (Figure 2J) as well as between spine apparatus area and spine head size (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: There is a positive correlation between spine apparatus area and spine head size in organotypic tissue cultures.
source: Finally, correlation analysis of SP cluster size and spine head size demonstrated a positive correlation between the two parameters (Figure 2J) as well as between spine apparatus area and spine head size (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Granule cells in organotypic tissue cultures are highly similar to granule cells in vivo regarding SP expression and distribution.
source: We conclude from these observations that regarding SP expression and distribution, granule cells in organotypic tissue cultures are highly similar to granule cells in vivo (c.f. Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: There is a robust correlation between increases in spine head size and insertion of SP.
source: This analysis revealed a robust correlation between increases in spine head size and insertion of SP and decreases of spine head size and loss of SP from spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a robust correlation between decreases of spine head size and loss of SP from spines.
source: This analysis revealed a robust correlation between increases in spine head size and insertion of SP and decreases of spine head size and loss of SP from spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mean maximum cross-sectional spine head area of spines that became SP+ increased significantly.
source: Sample spines (upper panels), mean spine head size changes (middle panels) and differences in spine head size of individual spines (lower panels) are illustrated. (A) Example of a spine that became SP+ (green or white co-localized with magenta spine) between day −1 and 0. The mean maximum cross-sectional spine head area of spines of this group increased significantly. ***p<0.0001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test. Number of spines n = 54.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mean maximum cross-sectional spine head area of spines that were SP+ and became SP- decreased significantly.
source: (B) Example of a spine that was SP+ and became SP- between day −1 and 0. The mean maximum cross-sectional spine head area of spines of this group decreased significantly. ***p<0.0001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test. Number of spines n = 52.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean cross-sectional spine head area of spines that remained SP+ did not change significantly.
source: (C) Example of a spine that remained SP+. The mean cross-sectional spine head area of spines of this group did not change significantly. p=0.850, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test. Number of spines n = 33.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mean cross-sectional spine head area of spines that remained SP- did not change significantly.
source: (D) Example of a spine that remained SP-. The mean cross-sectional spine head area of spines of this group did not change significantly. p=0.060, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test. Number of spines n = 340.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The median survival time of SP+ spines was approximately 17.5 days.
source: This analysis revealed major differences in the survival time of SP+ and SP- spines (Figure 4C–E): Whereas the median survival time of SP+ spines was ~17.5 days, the median survival time of SP- spines was only ~6.8 days (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The median survival time of SP- spines was approximately 6.8 days.
source: This analysis revealed major differences in the survival time of SP+ and SP- spines (Figure 4C–E): Whereas the median survival time of SP+ spines was ~17.5 days, the median survival time of SP- spines was only ~6.8 days (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SP- spines followed a single-phase exponential decay function.
source: In addition to this notable difference in median survival time, the curves that fitted our data turned out to be fundamentally different: Whereas SP- spines followed a single-phase exponential decay function, the decay of SP+ spines could only be fitted using a conditional two-stage exponential decay function (see below; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling of the survival data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The decay of SP+ spines could only be fitted using a conditional two-stage exponential decay function.
source: In addition to this notable difference in median survival time, the curves that fitted our data turned out to be fundamentally different: Whereas SP- spines followed a single-phase exponential decay function, the decay of SP+ spines could only be fitted using a conditional two-stage exponential decay function (see below; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling of the survival data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SP- and SP+ spines differ significantly in their survival times.
source: Finally, a data-driven simulation of spine survival was performed to test whether the survival times of the two spine populations are different. This approach revealed – within the parameters used – that SP- and SP+ spines differ significantly in their survival times (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulation shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The difference in spine survival between SP+ and SP- spines was still observed when comparing spines of equal head size.
source: We controlled for this possibility by comparing the survival times of SP+ and SP- spines of equal head size (matched pairs; Figure 4G). Even under these highly constrained conditions, the difference in spine survival between SP+ and SP- spines was still observed (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the size-matched analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The median survival of size-matched SP- spines was approximately 6.5 days.
source: The median survival of SP- spines of this population was ≈ 6.5 days, whereas size-matched SP+ spines showed a median survival of ≈ 16.7 days.
evidence: This is a finding from the size-matched analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Size-matched SP+ spines showed a median survival of approximately 16.7 days.
source: The median survival of SP- spines of this population was ≈ 6.5 days, whereas size-matched SP+ spines showed a median survival of ≈ 16.7 days.
evidence: This is a finding from the size-matched analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The survival curve of 'timed' SP+ spines was highly similar to the curve of the total population of SP+ spines.
source: Finally, we tested whether the time point at which SP had entered a spine plays a role. For this we compared 'timed' SP+ spines, which had just become SP+ (between day −1 and 0) with SP- spines that had stayed SP- (between day −1 and 0). The survival curve of these 'timed' SP+ spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) was again highly similar to the curve of the total population of SP+ spines (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of timed SP+ spines shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SP is tightly associated with the population of large and stable spines and rare in the group of small and less stable spines.
source: This appeared to be a possibility since SP is tightly associated with the population of large and stable spines and rare in the group of small and less stable spines (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: SP was completely absent from the very small spine group, in which approximately 41% of all SP- spines are found.
source: SP was completely absent from the very small spine group, in which ~ 41% of all SP- spines are found (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Very small SP- spines rapidly decayed with time following a single exponential decay function.
source: This spine population rapidly decayed with time following a single exponential decay function (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: Small SP- spines followed a single exponential decay curve with a median survival of approximately 7.8 days.
source: (G) Survival curves of small SP- and SP+ spines (examples shown). SP- spines (blue line; median survival ≈ 7.8 days) followed a single exponential decay curve, SP+ spines (red line; median survival ≈ 12.8 days) followed a conditional two-stage decay curve.
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Small SP+ spines followed a conditional two-stage decay curve with a median survival of approximately 12.8 days.
source: (G) Survival curves of small SP- and SP+ spines (examples shown). SP- spines (blue line; median survival ≈ 7.8 days) followed a single exponential decay curve, SP+ spines (red line; median survival ≈ 12.8 days) followed a conditional two-stage decay curve.
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Medium-sized SP- spines followed a single exponential decay curve with a median survival of approximately 6.9 days.
source: (K) Survival curves of medium-sized SP- and SP+ spines (examples shown). SP- spines (blue line; median survival ≈ 6.9 days) followed a single exponential decay curve, SP+ spines (red line; median survival ≈ 12.9 days) followed a conditional two-stage decay curve.
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Medium-sized SP+ spines followed a conditional two-stage decay curve with a median survival of approximately 12.9 days.
source: (K) Survival curves of medium-sized SP- and SP+ spines (examples shown). SP- spines (blue line; median survival ≈ 6.9 days) followed a single exponential decay curve, SP+ spines (red line; median survival ≈ 12.9 days) followed a conditional two-stage decay curve.
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Small and medium-sized spines survive longer and follow a conditional two-stage decay kinetic if SP is present.
source: We conclude from these data that small and medium-sized spines survive longer and follow a conditional two-stage decay kinetic if SP is present.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the survival analyses of small and medium-sized spines.

claim: Large spines account for approximately 4.9% of all spines.
source: Finally, we looked at the population of large spines. Although these spines only account for ~4.9% of all spines, they are considered especially important in the context of memory storage (Segal, 2005; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010; Abdou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Large spines are considered especially important in the context of memory storage.
source: Finally, we looked at the population of large spines. Although these spines only account for ~4.9% of all spines, they are considered especially important in the context of memory storage (Segal, 2005; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010; Abdou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: In the large spine group, only approximately 1.7% of the SP- spines are found whereas approximately 43% of SP+ spines are part of this subgroup.
source: In this group of spines only ~1.7% of the SP- spines are found whereas ~43% of SP+ spines are part of this subgroup.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: SP+ spines represent approximately 65% of the spines in the large spine size group.
source: SP+ spines represent ~65% of the spines in this size group.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Large SP- spines followed a single exponential function.
source: Comparing spine pairs of equal head sizes (Figure 5O) major differences in their survival and decay kinetics were revealed: Whereas SP-spines followed a single exponential function, SP+ spines were best modeled using the conditional two-stage decay function (Figure 5P–S).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis of large spines shown in Figure 5P-S.

claim: Large SP+ spines were best modeled using the conditional two-stage decay function.
source: Comparing spine pairs of equal head sizes (Figure 5O) major differences in their survival and decay kinetics were revealed: Whereas SP-spines followed a single exponential function, SP+ spines were best modeled using the conditional two-stage decay function (Figure 5P–S).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis of large spines shown in Figure 5P-S.

claim: Large SP- spines are pruned fast, with survival comparable to that of very small, small and medium-sized spines.
source: We conclude that large SP- spines are pruned fast. Their survival is comparable to that of very small (Figure 5C), small (Figure 5G) and medium-sized (Figure 5K) spines, suggesting that it is the presence of SP within spines rather than spine size per se which determines long-term spine survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the survival analyses across different spine sizes.

claim: It is the presence of SP within spines rather than spine size per se which determines long-term spine survival.
source: We conclude that large SP- spines are pruned fast. Their survival is comparable to that of very small (Figure 5C), small (Figure 5G) and medium-sized (Figure 5K) spines, suggesting that it is the presence of SP within spines rather than spine size per se which determines long-term spine survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the survival analyses across different spine sizes.

claim: The distribution of spines of the eGFP-SP-tg and the SP-KO mice was comparable across the four size categories.
source: First, we compared the distribution of spines of the eGFP-SP-tg and the SP-KO mice and found comparable fractions of spines in the four size categories (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SP-deficient spines and SP- spines behave very similar with regard to their survival times and decay kinetics in each of the four size groups.
source: Next, we compared SP-deficient spines to SP- spines and found that these two groups of spines behave very similar with regard to their survival times and decay kinetics in each of the four size groups (Figure 6B–R): survival times were similar and all curves followed single exponential decay functions.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison shown in Figure 6B-R.

claim: The 'spine phenotype' associated with SP-deficiency does not result in altered spine geometry but in altered spine survival.
source: This demonstrates that the 'spine phenotype' associated with SP-deficiency does not result in altered spine geometry but in altered spine survival, that is spine stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of SP-deficient and SP- spines.

claim: Spine formation was significantly higher in SP-KO dendrites as compared to eGFP-SP-tg dendrites.
source: (A) Spine formation was significantly higher in SP-KO dendrites as compared to eGFP-SP-tg dendrites. **p=0.0011, Mann–Whitney U-test. Number of dendritic segments: eGFP-SP-tg, n = 24; SP-KO, n = 21.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Spine turnover ratio was significantly higher in SP-KO dendrites as compared to eGFP-SP-tg dendrites over the two-week observation period.
source: (C) Spine turnover ratio was significantly higher in SP-KO dendrites as compared to eGFP-SP-tg dendrites over the two-week observation period. ***p=0.0003, Mann–Whitney U-test. Number of dendritic segments: eGFP-SP-tg, n = 24; SP-KO, n = 21.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduced stability of large spines will have to be homeostatically compensated by an increased formation of spines and an increased spine turnover.
source: We then wondered how the lack of the stable SP+ spine population affects spine dynamics, in particular spine turnover, of the SP-deficient animals. We reasoned that the reduced stability of large spines will have to be homeostatically compensated by an increased formation of spines and an increased spine turnover.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated before testing it experimentally.

claim: SP-deficient mutants show a compensatory increase in spine turnover.
source: Indeed, these dynamic parameters were significantly increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), revealing a yet unknown and most likely compensatory phenotype of the SP-deficient mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the group of initially SP+ spines the fraction of SP+ spines decreased with time, whereas the fraction of SP- spines increased.
source: This analysis revealed that in the group of initially SP+ spines the fraction of SP+ spines decreased with time, whereas the fraction of SP- spines increased. This was followed by an increase in the fraction of lost spines (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the group of the initially SP- spines the fraction of surviving spines decreased much more rapidly.
source: In the group of the initially SP- spines the fraction of surviving spines decreased much more rapidly (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: At the observation endpoint (day 12), approximately 59% of spines which were initially SP+ survived.
source: At the observation endpoint (day 12), ~59% of spines which were initially SP+ survived (Figure 7C), whereas only ~33% of spines which were initially SP- were still present (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At the observation endpoint (day 12), only approximately 33% of spines which were initially SP- were still present.
source: At the observation endpoint (day 12), ~59% of spines which were initially SP+ survived (Figure 7C), whereas only ~33% of spines which were initially SP- were still present (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The size of the surviving SP+ spines did not change significantly during the two-week observation period.
source: The size of the surviving SP+ (Figure 7E) and SP- (Figure 7F) spines did not change significantly during the two-week observation period, in line with our finding that spine head size per se is not the major determinant of spine stability.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The size of the surviving SP- spines did not change significantly during the two-week observation period.
source: The size of the surviving SP+ (Figure 7E) and SP- (Figure 7F) spines did not change significantly during the two-week observation period, in line with our finding that spine head size per se is not the major determinant of spine stability.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: All spines that were lost within one day (between days −1 and 0) were SP-.
source: First, we determined the SP content of the 16% of spines that were lost within one day, that is between days −1 and 0. All of these pruned spines were SP-, in line with our hypothesis (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Of spines that were initially SP+ and were pruned during the observation period, approximately 94% were SP- prior to their pruning.
source: Next, we predicted that SP+ spines should not be lost without going through a SP- state. For this analysis, we looked at all spines that were initially SP+, that is spines SP+ at day 0, and focused on those SP+ spines that were pruned sometime during the observation period. Of these spines ~ 94% were SP- prior to their pruning (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Several SP+ spines (n = 10) undulated between a SP+ and SP- state.
source: This hypothesis could be falsified since we observed several SP+ spines (n = 10) undulating between a SP+ and SP- state (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: SP can be removed from a spine and reintroduced into a spine without the spine being pruned.
source: Thus, SP can be removed from a spine and reintroduced into a spine without the spine being pruned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of undulating spines.

claim: Changes in SP content were accompanied by bidirectional changes in head size.
source: Of note, the changes in SP content were accompanied by bidirectional changes in head size (Figure 7I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of a SP cluster from a spine does not cause pruning of that spine.
source: Taken together, we conclude from these observations that loss of a SP cluster from a spine does not cause pruning of that spine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of undulating spines.

claim: Denervation results in a profound destabilization of denervated granule cell spines.
source: To address this question, we transected the entorhinal axons, that is the so-called perforant path, innervating the distal two-thirds of the dendritic tree of dentate granule cells (Figure 8A; Del Turco and Deller, 2007). This results in a profound destabilization of denervated granule cell spines (Vlachos et al., 2012; Vlachos et al., 2013a), making it possible to study the effect of SP remaining within the postsynaptic compartment on spine stability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Denervation greatly accelerated spine loss.
source: As shown previously (Vlachos et al., 2012), denervation greatly accelerated spine loss (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the denervation experiments shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Following denervation, median survival of SP+ spines dropped from 17.5 days in controls to 6.5 days.
source: This increase in spine loss was observed for both SP+ as well as SP- spines: In the case of the SP+ spines, median survival dropped from 17.5 days in controls to 6.5 days following denervation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the denervation experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Following denervation, median survival of SP- spines dropped from 6.8 days in controls to 3.4 days.
source: Similarly, median survival of SP- spines dropped from 6.8 days in controls to 3.4 days following denervation (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a finding from the denervation experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: After denervation, denervated SP- spines followed a single-phase exponential decay function.
source: As in controls, denervated SP- spines followed a single-phase exponential decay function and SP+ spines followed a conditional two-stage exponential decay function.
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling of the denervation data.

claim: After denervation, SP+ spines followed a conditional two-stage exponential decay function.
source: As in controls, denervated SP- spines followed a single-phase exponential decay function and SP+ spines followed a conditional two-stage exponential decay function.
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling of the denervation data.

claim: Although denervation greatly accelerated the decay of both groups, SP+ spines were still significantly more stable than their SP- size-matched counterparts.
source: Finally, we compared denervated SP+ with denervated SP- spines (Figure 8I–M). To control for any effects of spine head size, size-matched spines were used (Figure 8I). Although denervation greatly accelerated the decay of both groups, SP+ spines were still significantly more stable than their SP- size-matched counterparts.
evidence: This is a finding from the denervation experiments shown in Figure 8I-M.

claim: The presence of SP within the postsynaptic spine compartment is still associated with higher spine stability, even in the absence of a presynaptic element.
source: From these data we conclude that the presence of SP within the postsynaptic spine compartment is still associated with higher spine stability, even in the absence of a presynaptic element.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the denervation experiments.

claim: The decay curves of SP- and SP+ spines are non-overlapping and mathematically distinct.
source: The decay curves of SP- and SP+ spines (Figures 4 and 5) are non-overlapping and mathematically distinct, since they cannot be trivially transformed into each other, for example using a scaling factor.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The survival curve of SP- spines can be simulated and fit using a single-phase exponential decay function.
source: We first analyzed the survival curve of SP- spines, which we could readily simulate and fit to our data using a single-phase exponential decay function
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the mathematical modeling.

claim: τspine of SP- spines is approximately 9.8 days and the half-life of these spines is approximately 6.8 days.
source: Fitting the data to this model, τspine of SP- spines is ~9.8 days and the half-life of these spines is ~6.8 days (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4.

claim: An almost perfect fit for SP+ spine survival could be obtained by using a conditional two-stage exponential decay function, identical to the one used to model the conditional two-stage decay of radioisotopes.
source: An almost perfect fit could be obtained, however, by using a conditional two-stage exponential decay function, identical to the one used to model the conditional two-stage decay of radioisotopes (Bateman, 1910).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the mathematical modeling with a citation.

claim: The time constant τSP of the first decay process (SP+ spines becoming SP-) is approximately 11.1 days and the half-life of SP in spines is approximately 7.7 days.
source: We fitted the survival data for SP+ spines to this equation and found the time constant τSP of the first decay process (SP+ spines becoming SP-) to be ~11.1 days and accordingly the half-life of SP in spines to be ~7.7 days.
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling.

claim: After approximately 17.4 days, approximately 50% of all initially SP+ spines would have disappeared.
source: Thus, after approximately 17.4 days, ~50% of all initially SP+ spines would have disappeared (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4.

claim: The survival curves of SP+ spines are compatible with a conditional two-stage decay process in which SP+ spines first lose their SP cluster (τSP) before being subsequently pruned as SP- spines with the time constant (τspine).
source: We conclude from this mathematical analysis of our experimental data that the survival curves of SP+ spines are compatible with a conditional two-stage decay process in which SP+ spines first lose their SP cluster (τSP) before being subsequently pruned as SP- spines with the time constant (τspine; same as initially SP- spines; Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling shown in Figure 9.

claim: SP is primarily present in large spines.
source: Our major findings can be summarized as follows: (1) SP is primarily present in large spines.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding in the discussion.

claim: SP+ spines of all sizes are more stable than SP- spines.
source: (2) SP+ spines of all sizes are more stable than SP- spines.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding in the discussion.

claim: Spines of SP-deficient animals decay like SP- spines.
source: (3) Spines of SP-deficient animals decay like SP- spines. In these mutants, a compensatory increase in spine turnover is observed.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding in the discussion.

claim: In SP-deficient mutants, a compensatory increase in spine turnover is observed.
source: (3) Spines of SP-deficient animals decay like SP- spines. In these mutants, a compensatory increase in spine turnover is observed.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding in the discussion.

claim: SP+ spines that later underwent pruning passed through a SP- state and followed a conditional two-stage decay kinetic.
source: (4) SP+ spines that later underwent pruning passed through a SP- state. These spines followed a conditional two-stage decay kinetic.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding in the discussion.

claim: SP+ spines are more stable than SP- spines following denervation.
source: (5) SP+ spines are more stable than SP- spines following denervation.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding in the discussion.

claim: SP is a major regulator of spine stability.
source: Together, our results implicate SP as a major regulator of spine stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: The presence of SP in large spines could explain their higher stability.
source: Since SP is present in ~65% of large (>0.8 µm2) spines, its presence in these spines could explain their higher stability (e.g., Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Kasai et al., 2010; McKinney, 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion with citations.

claim: Roles of SP in spine head expansion and in the maintenance of an expanded spine head were suggested.
source: After effects of SP on spine density and spine length were ruled out (Deller et al., 2003), roles in spine head expansion (Zhang et al., 2013) and in the maintenance of an expanded spine head (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Konietzny et al., 2019) were suggested.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: It is not the size of a spine per se that is important for stability but rather the presence of SP within a spine.
source: This conclusion is supported by the following observations: (1) Small spines (0.3–0.55 µm2 head area) containing SP have a long lifetime and a median survival of 12.8 days. Large spines (>0.8 µm2 head area) without SP have a median survival time of 7.7 days. Thus, small SP+ spines are more stable than large SP- spines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: Small SP+ spines are more stable than large SP- spines.
source: This conclusion is supported by the following observations: (1) Small spines (0.3–0.55 µm2 head area) containing SP have a long lifetime and a median survival of 12.8 days. Large spines (>0.8 µm2 head area) without SP have a median survival time of 7.7 days. Thus, small SP+ spines are more stable than large SP- spines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: The median survival time of SP- spines was similar among all size groups (very small, small, medium and large) and much shorter than the median survival time of SP+ spines of any size.
source: (2) Comparison of the median survival times of SP- spines revealed that their median survival time was similar among all size groups (i.e., very small, small, medium and large) and much shorter than the median survival time of SP+ spines of any size.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: All spines, including the large spines, of SP-deficient animals decayed like SP- spines and had short median survival times.
source: Finally, (3) all spines, including the large spines, of SP-deficient animals decayed like SP- spines and had short median survival times.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: The presence of SP within a spine is a much more reliable indicator of its stability than the size of its head.
source: Although this does not fully exclude a small effect of spine size on spine survival, for example large spines may need time to shrink prior to their removal (see next paragraph), our data show that the presence of SP within a spine is a much more reliable indicator of its stability than the size of its head.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: Removal of the spine stabilizing protein SP is a necessary step before the actin cytoskeleton of a spine can be degraded and the spine can be pruned.
source: Second, by following SP+ spines that were pruned during the observation period, we could show that in almost all cases, these spines went through a SP- state before they disappeared. Thus, our data suggest that removal of the spine stabilizing protein SP is a necessary step before the actin cytoskeleton of a spine can be degraded and the spine can be pruned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: Spines losing SP also shrank in size.
source: Third, in line with the fact that SP is associated with large spines, we observed that spines losing SP also shrank in size (Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: SP+ spines designated to be pruned follow a conditional two-stage decay function.
source: In agreement with these observations, we found that SP+ spines designated to be pruned follow a conditional two-stage decay function, similar to the one described for radioactive isotopes in Physics (Bateman, 1910): The first stage is the slow 'decay' of SP+ spines into a SP- state. The second stage is the pruning of these SP- spines, which goes as fast as for initially SP- spines (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study in the discussion with a citation.

claim: SP-deficient granule cells compensated for the reduced stability of spines by increasing their spine formation and thereby their spine turnover ratio.
source: In addition, SP-deficient granule cells compensated for the reduced stability of spines by increasing their spine formation and thereby their spine turnover ratio.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study in the discussion.

claim: SP-deficient neurons homeostatically compensate for the loss of stability by upregulating their spine formation.
source: This finding suggests that SP-deficient neurons homeostatically compensate for the loss of stability by upregulating their spine formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion.

claim: Loss or overexpression of SP does not seem to affect spine densities.
source: This may explain why loss or overexpression of SP does not seem to affect spine densities (Deller et al., 2003; Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP appears to be a major regulator of spine stability.
source: Whereas spine density appears to be regulated by other molecules, including among others hormones (Woolley, 2000; Segal and Murphy, 2001; Fester et al., 2012; Luine and Frankfurt, 2012), actin-modulating proteins (Yamazaki et al., 2014), Fragile X mental retardation protein (Irwin et al., 2000; Bagni and Zukin, 2019), non-coding RNAs (Briz et al., 2017), neurotrophic factors (Murphy et al., 1998) and adhesion molecules (Segura et al., 2007; Keeler et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2017), SP appears to be a major regulator of spine stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings in the discussion with citations.

claim: The preferential localization of SP clusters in the lower part of the spine head argues for an association of SP with the stable pool of actin.
source: In comparison to other well-established stabilizers of spines, such as PSD-95 (El-Husseini et al., 2000; Cane et al., 2014), which primarily act at the synapse (Ehrlich et al., 2007; De Roo et al., 2008; Yoshihara et al., 2009; Meyer et al., 2014), the preferential localization of SP clusters in the lower part of the spine head argues for an association of SP with the stable pool of actin, which forms the central and less dynamic core of spines (Bramham et al., 2008; Bosch et al., 2014; Colgan and Yasuda, 2014; Spence and Soderling, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings in the discussion with citations.

claim: SP directly binds to actin and can induce actin aggregates.
source: Extant data suggest that a stabilizing effect of SP on actin can be caused by several direct and indirect interactions: (i) SP directly binds to actin and can induce actin aggregates (Mundel et al., 1997; Asanuma et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP interacts with alpha-actinin-2 and in the presence of both proteins long, unbranched and highly stable actin filaments are formed.
source: (ii) SP interacts with alpha-actinin-2 and in the presence of both proteins long, unbranched and highly stable actin filaments are formed (Asanuma et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP protects actin filaments from disruption.
source: (iii) SP protects actin filaments from disruption (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2016), potentially by blocking signals inducing actin fragmentation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: For kidney podocytes, interactions of SP with Rho-GTPase family members have been reported.
source: For kidney podocytes, interactions of SP with Rho-GTPase family members have been reported (Asanuma et al., 2006; Yanagida-Asanuma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: In neurons, Rho-GTPases regulate the maintenance of spines and RhoA in particular promotes prolonged spine enlargement.
source: In neurons, Rho-GTPases regulate the maintenance of spines and RhoA in particular promotes prolonged spine enlargement (Tashiro and Yuste, 2008; Murakoshi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: By protecting RhoA from proteasomal degradation, SP could increase spine stability.
source: By protecting RhoA from proteasomal degradation (Asanuma et al., 2006), SP could increase spine stability.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with a citation in the discussion.

claim: SP may stabilize spines indirectly via the spine apparatus organelle and its function as a Ca2+ store.
source: (iv) Finally, SP may stabilize spines indirectly via the spine apparatus organelle and its function as a Ca2+ store (Korkotian and Segal, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with a citation in the discussion.

claim: Higher Ca2+ transients could stabilize spines via the postsynaptic Ca2+-sensor caldendrin.
source: Higher Ca2+ transients could stabilize spines via the postsynaptic Ca2+-sensor caldendrin (Mikhaylova et al., 2018), or via activation of kinases, which, in turn, inactivate actin-depolymerizing proteins such as cofilin (see Borovac et al., 2018, for review).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations in the discussion.

claim: Cofilin and SP are found in similar locations within the spine compartment.
source: Of note, cofilin (Bosch et al., 2014; Borovac et al., 2018) and SP (this study; Bas Orth et al., 2005) are found in similar locations within the spine compartment, hinting at some kind of crosstalk between these proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP could influence the stability of actin pools and/or actin treadmilling in spines via several mutually non-exclusive direct and indirect mechanism.
source: In sum, SP could influence the stability of actin pools and/or actin treadmilling in spines via several mutually non-exclusive direct and indirect mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion of potential mechanisms.

claim: SP plays an important role in Hebbian and homeostatic forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: SP plays an important role in Hebbian- (Yamazaki et al., 2001; Deller et al., 2003; Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Holbro et al., 2009; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013; Jedlicka and Deller, 2017) and homeostatic (Vlachos et al., 2013b) forms of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: Under conditions of synaptic strengthening SP is upregulated.
source: Under conditions of synaptic strengthening SP is upregulated (Yamazaki et al., 2001), sorted within neurons (Fukazawa et al., 2003) and recruited into activated spines (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP is sorted within neurons under conditions of synaptic strengthening.
source: Under conditions of synaptic strengthening SP is upregulated (Yamazaki et al., 2001), sorted within neurons (Fukazawa et al., 2003) and recruited into activated spines (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP is recruited into activated spines under conditions of synaptic strengthening.
source: Under conditions of synaptic strengthening SP is upregulated (Yamazaki et al., 2001), sorted within neurons (Fukazawa et al., 2003) and recruited into activated spines (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: In the context of Hebbian plasticity, SP appears to be part of the downstream machinery executing functional and structural changes.
source: In the context of Hebbian plasticity, SP appears to be part of the downstream machinery executing functional and structural changes (see Jedlicka and Deller, 2017, for review).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with a citation in the discussion.

claim: At the functional level, SP plays an important role as an essential molecule of the spine apparatus organelle, which acts as a local calcium source and sink.
source: At the functional level, SP plays an important role as an essential molecule of the spine apparatus organelle, which acts as a local calcium source and sink (Vlachos et al., 2009; Korkotian and Segal, 2011; Korkotian et al., 2014) and which regulates AMPA-R trafficking to excitatory postsynapses (Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: The spine apparatus regulates AMPA-R trafficking to excitatory postsynapses.
source: At the functional level, SP plays an important role as an essential molecule of the spine apparatus organelle, which acts as a local calcium source and sink (Vlachos et al., 2009; Korkotian and Segal, 2011; Korkotian et al., 2014) and which regulates AMPA-R trafficking to excitatory postsynapses (Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: At the structural level, SP is recruited to enlarged spines and increases their stability.
source: At the structural level, it is recruited to enlarged spines (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008; Vlachos et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013) and increases their stability (this study).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP+ spines are large and strong spines exhibiting a high density of AMPA-R.
source: Since SP+ spines are large and strong spines exhibiting a high density of AMPA-R (Vlachos et al., 2009), loss of SP from only this fraction of spines suffices to impair Hebbian plasticity (Deller et al., 2003; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013; Grigoryan and Segal, 2016), underlining its role in Hebbian forms of synaptic strengthening.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: Loss of SP from only the fraction of SP+ spines suffices to impair Hebbian plasticity.
source: Since SP+ spines are large and strong spines exhibiting a high density of AMPA-R (Vlachos et al., 2009), loss of SP from only this fraction of spines suffices to impair Hebbian plasticity (Deller et al., 2003; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013; Grigoryan and Segal, 2016), underlining its role in Hebbian forms of synaptic strengthening.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citations in the discussion.

claim: Prior to learning, spines are dynamic and rapidly turned over.
source: At the behavioral level, learning has been linked to spine stability: Prior to learning, spines are dynamic and rapidly turned over. After instructive experience, however, spines are more stable and their synapses have been strengthened (Roberts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation in the discussion.

claim: After instructive experience, spines are more stable and their synapses have been strengthened.
source: At the behavioral level, learning has been linked to spine stability: Prior to learning, spines are dynamic and rapidly turned over. After instructive experience, however, spines are more stable and their synapses have been strengthened (Roberts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation in the discussion.

claim: At the network level, neuronal ensemble formation and long-term memory require strong and stable synapses.
source: Similarly, at the network level, neuronal ensemble formation and long-term memory require strong and stable synapses (Kasai et al., 2010; Koleske, 2013; Rogerson et al., 2014; Segal, 2017; Yokose et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: Synapses requiring a high degree of stability, for example synapses after a learning experience or synapses binding excitatory neurons together into functional ensembles, may require SP as their stabilizer.
source: In the present study, we have linked the stability of spines to the presence of the actin-modulating protein SP. This makes it attractive to speculate that synapses requiring a high degree of stability, for example synapses after a learning experience (Roberts et al., 2010) or synapses binding excitatory neurons together into functional ensembles (Yokose et al., 2017), require SP as their stabilizer.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations in the discussion.

claim: A reduction in spine stability has been reported in aged and pathologically altered brains.
source: Conversely, a reduction in spine stability has been reported in aged (Voglewede et al., 2019) and pathologically altered brains (Halpain et al., 2005; Spires-Jones et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: SP is reduced in aged and pathologically altered brains.
source: Since SP is reduced under these conditions (Reddy et al., 2005; Counts et al., 2014; Sidhu et al., 2016; Wingo et al., 2019), it is conceivable that insufficient levels of SP could contribute to brain pathologies in which network stability is reduced.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations in the discussion.

claim: Insufficient levels of SP could contribute to brain pathologies in which network stability is reduced.
source: Since SP is reduced under these conditions (Reddy et al., 2005; Counts et al., 2014; Sidhu et al., 2016; Wingo et al., 2019), it is conceivable that insufficient levels of SP could contribute to brain pathologies in which network stability is reduced.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations in the discussion.
